summary: David Walden notes that the new message-id bits from RFC 533 give lost message detection almost for free, since the four extra bits can act like the sequence number Hathaway proposed in RFC 512, and describes three ways hosts can use them. It builds on RFC 512 and RFC 516.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 534 explains how the message-id field described in RFC 533 could help hosts detect missing messages. If both hosts use matching sequence numbers, they can identify a gap and choose how to retransmit.

questions: how to detect lost messages with message-id
what is a 16 element sequence number in the imp
subtitle: How the message-id bits could help hosts detect lost messages and retransmit them.

tldr.problem: Hosts need a way to notice when a message sent over a connection has been lost.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes treating the four added message-id bits as a 16-element sequence per connection, with zero indicating that sequence numbers are not in use.
tldr.outcome: It describes three ways to use the field and explains that synchronized IDs can support loss detection and retransmission strategies.

facts.label: Sequence element zero
facts.value: Indicates sequence numbers are not in use

today: The unit records RFC 534's status as Unknown and lists no updates or obsoleting RFCs. It discusses possible uses of the message-id field described in RFC 533.

sections.title: Message IDs as Sequence Numbers
sections.content:
RFC 534 says the four added message-id bits can act as a sequence number for each connection if sending hosts use unique values and receiving hosts examine them. The resulting sequence has 16 elements. The RFC says this is enough because the IMPs allow no more than four outstanding messages at a time between a pair of hosts.

Sequence element zero can signal that the hosts are not using sequence numbers. This idea builds on lost-message detection approaches cited in RFCs 512 and 516.
sections.plainLanguage: Numbering messages lets a receiver notice when an expected number is missing. The receiver can do this only if it also looks at the numbers and the sender uses them consistently.

sections.title: Three Ways to Use the Field
sections.content:
The RFC describes three modes. A sender can set the extra bits to zero and send only one message at a time on a link, allowing orderly retransmission without receiver help but reducing speed. If the receiver gives no help, unique IDs can identify which message was lost, but the sender has no method for orderly retransmission.

In the third mode, the sender may have several messages outstanding and the receiver helps. If both sides use synchronized unique IDs, such as sequential numbers, the receiver can reliably detect lost messages.
sections.plainLanguage: With no receiver help, a sender can wait after each message or merely identify which message was lost. When the receiver helps and both sides synchronize IDs, it can detect a missing message.

sections.title: Possible Retransmission Strategies
sections.content:
The RFC gives two examples of how synchronized message IDs can support retransmission. The sender can resend the appropriate messages after an incomplete transmission, while the receiver uses the IDs to place them in the right order.

Alternatively, the receiver can discard messages that arrive out of order. The sender then backs up and retransmits the message associated with the incomplete transmission and all later messages.
sections.plainLanguage: A receiver can put retransmitted messages back in sequence, or discard out-of-order messages and ask the sender to start again from the gap.
